items.title: Kenny Davern interviewed by Monk Rowe, Clearwater Beach, Florida, March 16, 2001 [interview 2 of 2]
items.q: I made a conscious effort to play trios. So I did a trio with Art Hodes and Don DeMicheal, and then they died. And then it was Ralph Sutton and Gus Johnson and Gus Johnson died.

ctx.x: That’s something to sustain a band like that too without a bass player I think.

Oh we were brilliant. We really enjoyed. I made a conscious effort to play trios. So I did a trio with Art Hodes and Don DeMicheal, and then they died. And then it was Ralph Sutton and Gus Johnson and Gus Johnson died. Then I did one with Dick Wellstood and Bobby Rosengarden, and Dick died. And then, you know, but after a while, so like I switched to guitars. And they’re all alive. In fact we’re going to do it tonight, the Breezin’ Along group. I’ll have fun with that. Because Howard Alden can read my mind, Bucky…

items.title: 67559_Art Hodes oral history interview
items.q: Like our friend Kenny Davern says, five percent of the musicians in the country are making a livelihood out of music.

ctx.x: I suddenly found out that I wasn't going to get anything back, I was going to give them more. But it was a good feeling. All this came through these TV shows, admittedly so. But there was also movement. Jazz was becoming more -- there was an audience growing up and there was things going on in jazz all over the country. There was something in Colorado going on, there was something in Odessa, Texas, there was something in Decatur, there's something in Manassas. There are suddenly festivals.

And then the European scene opened up. And all this helped make for more work for a select few musicians. Like our friend Kenny Davern says, five percent of the musicians in the country are making a livelihood out of music. Now, take that five percent and figure out how many of them are jazz musicians. And you will find that in New York City, if you find 50 you've found quite a few that are making it strictly playing jazz. And in Chicago, two, three, one, four, how many? Playing jazz. I'm not thinking about --
